title: Friends without benefits: Why the EU should offer Canada more than casual defence ties – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: With Carney declaring Canada “at war” with the US over trade and Trump renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America”, ECFR argues the EU should give Canada Ukraine-style carve-outs in its defence-industrial programmes — writing Ottawa into the European Competitiveness Fund's defence window — in exchange for paid access, reciprocal procurement and aligned export controls. Canada's 2%-of-GDP defence budget already exceeds the 14 smallest EU budgets combined and is heading to 4% by 2030.

themes.theme: Canada as an underrated defence market

insights.claim: Canada's current 2%-of-GDP defence spending already exceeds the 14 smallest EU defence budgets combined and ranks behind only Germany, France, Italy and Poland among European-scale spenders.
insights.so_what: Reframes Canada from junior partner to a top-five-scale European defence customer — material for EU primes assessing addressable demand.
insights.quote: The 2% of its GDP that it currently spends on defence is already more than the 14 smallest EU defence budgets combined
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Canada is moving to spend 4% of GDP on defence by 2030 and C$500bn (€310bn) over the next decade, much of it on equipment and suppliers outside Canada.
insights.so_what: A decade-scale procurement pool that is explicitly open to non-domestic suppliers — the size of the prize for European defence exporters.
insights.locator: And its budget is set to increase significantly
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Carney has said explicitly that “the days of our military sending 70 cents of every dollar to the United States are over”, signalling a deliberate diversion of Canadian procurement away from US primes.
insights.so_what: A named, quantified share of Canadian procurement in play — negative for US defence exporters, positive for European and Nordic ones.
insights.quote: The days of our military sending 70 cents of every dollar to the United States are over.
insights.locator: Much of that money will be invested in equipment
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: German shipbuilder ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems has won the contest to build 12 submarines for the Royal Canadian Navy, the biggest defence deal in Canadian history, while Canada is weighing Swedish Gripen fighters instead of American F-35s and is building icebreakers in Helsinki.
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence the substitution away from US kit is already happening — a live template for other US allies diversifying suppliers.
insights.locator: On the procurement side, German shipbuilder ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Canada brings capabilities Europe lacks: Arctic warfare know-how and six decades inside NORAD giving it rare continental-scale air-defence and early-warning experience, just as Europeans scramble to build an independent missile-defence network.
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific capability gaps where Canadian participation would accelerate European air and missile defence programmes.
insights.locator: Canada’s armed forces bring significant know-how in Arctic warfare
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

themes.theme: Rule arbitrage in EU defence funding

insights.claim: Under current EDIP rules a system built in Europe carrying 35% American components qualifies for EU funding while a wholly Canadian one does not, and those rules will likely roll over unchanged into the European Competitiveness Fund.
insights.so_what: A precise regulatory anomaly that determines which supply chains get EU money — the rule to watch in the next EU budget negotiation.
insights.quote: Under those rules, a system built in Europe carrying 35% American components would qualify for funding, but a wholly Canadian one would not.
insights.locator: As it stands, current EDIP rules will likely roll over
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Ukraine has already received carve-outs from EDIP and from SAFE — the EU mechanism offering €150bn in low-interest defence loans — proving the EU will bend third-country rules, so the question is only what circumstances justify it.
insights.so_what: Establishes the precedent argument that will be used for Britain, Norway and Canada — a template for widening access to EU defence money.
insights.locator: The EU already treats one non-member as something more
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Access should not be free: Canada should pay for entry, open its own procurement to European firms and align its export controls with the EU's, with a proof-of-concept major system containing no US export-controlled parts — a counter-drone system would work well.
insights.so_what: The ITAR-free system is the actionable concept here — a European-Canadian counter-drone programme free of US export control would be a distinct new product category.
insights.locator: These would be major concessions and they must not be given away for free
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Low-friction entry points exist now: Canada could join the PESCO projects ACCESS (Arctic-capable, GPS-denied electronic warfare and sensors) and TWISTER's space-based early warning strand without an EDA arrangement, since neither is EDA-supported.
insights.so_what: Names the specific programmes where Canadian money and technology could arrive fastest — near-term contract visibility.
insights.locator: A first step would be encouraging Canada to join further PESCO projects
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Berlin and Paris should back Canada's proposed Defence Security and Resilience Bank and could merge it with Britain's proposed Multilateral Defence Mechanism to create a financing coalition spanning Britain, Canada and EU member states.
insights.so_what: A potential new multilateral defence-financing institution outside EU structures — watch for it at the October EU-Canada summit.
insights.locator: In addition to these efforts, Berlin and Paris should also throw their weight
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

themes.theme: The transatlantic cost of blurring the lines

insights.claim: Carney announced on August 22nd that Canada was “at war” with the United States after trade negotiations collapsed at the eleventh hour, and Trump then renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing the January Greenland sovereignty crisis.
insights.so_what: The specific rupture that makes EU-Canada defence integration politically possible — US territorial rhetoric is now a live variable for allied procurement decisions.
insights.locator: European leaders losing sleep over Trump’s economic
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Elbridge Colby suspended the Permanent Joint Board on Defence, a longstanding US-Canadian consultative body, linking the pause to Canada's weak defence spending and its middle powers strategy, which Washington increasingly views as a challenge to its primacy.
insights.so_what: Concrete US retaliation already underway — a template for how Washington punishes middle-power coordination, and a risk to any EU-Canada deal.
insights.locator: The US has repeatedly cast scorn on Carney’s middle powers strategy
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union restricts membership to European states, but the EU does not have to choose between full membership and arm's-length third-country status — a strict in-or-out model would exclude Ukraine, Britain, Norway and Canada from the bloc's defence industrial base and leave Europe less safe.
insights.so_what: The conceptual move that would reshape who can bid for EU defence money — relevant to UK and Norwegian defence firms too.
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Canadian Armed Forces have modelled a possible US military invasion, just as Denmark flew blood bags to Greenland in anticipation of a US invasion in January.
insights.so_what: How seriously allied militaries now treat US territorial threats — a datum most transatlantic risk models still exclude.
insights.locator: Europeans shouldn’t scoff at Canadian concerns
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar

insights.claim: Inviting Canada into the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force, which sits outside NATO and EU structures, would involve little red tape and could happen almost immediately, improving non-US allied interoperability as Washington considers far-reaching troop reductions in Europe.
insights.so_what: The fastest available deliverable from the October summit and an early signal of how serious the de-risking really is.
insights.locator: An additional step which would contribute decisively
insights.speaker: Anand Sundar
